# `ClassFile.verify`: re-checking generated bytes and the limits of structural verification

> **Objective:** After generating or transforming bytecode with the **Java Class-File API**, know how to call `ClassFile.verify(...)` on **the exact newly generated byte data**, read the `VerifyError` list, distinguish class-file syntax errors from bytecode verification errors, recognize what this check **cannot guarantee**, and build a safe workflow before passing a new class into a class loader or Java agent.

This lesson belongs to the **Class-File API** group in Java Advanced Instrumentation. Examples use **JDK 24 or later**, because the standard `java.lang.classfile` API was finalized and officially released in **Java 24** (JEP 484). **Do not compile this example with Java 17**: Java 17 does not yet have the standard `java.lang.classfile.ClassFile` API. Experimental/preview releases prior to JDK 24 may differ in signatures or require preview flags; choose JDK 24+ for this hands-on lesson.

## 1. Why is "build succeeded" not enough?

When writing a Java agent, a processing flow typically looks like this:

```text
Original .class
      │
      ▼
ClassFile.parse(...) → ClassModel
      │
      ▼
Analysis / ClassTransform / ClassBuilder
      │
      ▼
byte[] candidate = newly generated bytes
      │
      ├── ClassFile.verify(candidate)
      │         ├── Errors found → report errors, do not pass to JVM
      │         └── No errors detected
      │
      ▼
Write .class or return byte[] to ClassFileTransformer
      │
      ▼
JVM loads/links/verifies, then program executes
```

Many class-file generation programs run through `ClassFile.build(...)` or `ClassFile.transformClass(...)` without throwing an exception. However, that **does not mean** every descriptor, control flow, operand stack, stack-map frame, and data relationship is valid. The Class-File API documentation explicitly states that builders/transformers **do not proactively perform all consistency checks** during construction. Some severe errors, such as an unbound label, may cause the builder to throw `IllegalArgumentException`; many other errors only surface during verification or when the JVM defines/links/runs the class.

If an agent returns invalid bytes to `ClassFileTransformer`, the error may only appear when the JVM loads the target class and break a running request. Therefore, the `verify` step is an **early-detection barrier**, not a formality.

**Central rule:** Check **the final candidate that will be released**, not just the original source bytes or the `ClassModel` before modification.

## 2. Scope of `ClassFile.verify`

The core of the API is the `java.lang.classfile.ClassFile` interface:

```java
ClassFile cf = ClassFile.of();
```

Three overloads are available:

```java
// Reference API signatures, not a standalone Java program:
List<VerifyError> verify(byte[] bytes);
List<VerifyError> verify(ClassModel model);
List<VerifyError> verify(Path path) throws IOException;
```

Where:

- **`verify(byte[])`**: directly checks a class-file byte array. This is the natural choice **right after `build`/`transformClass` and before returning bytes to the agent**.
- **`verify(ClassModel)`**: checks a parsed model; useful when analyzing a model, but **does not replace** checking the **final** generated `byte[]`.
- **`verify(Path)`**: reads and checks a `.class` file on disk. Useful for a build pipeline checking **the artifact actually written**; may throw `IOException` if reading the file fails.

All three return `List<java.lang.VerifyError>`:

```java
List<VerifyError> errors = ClassFile.of().verify(candidate);
if (!errors.isEmpty()) {
    for (VerifyError error : errors) {
        System.err.println(error);
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException("Generated class did not verify");
}
```

This logic snippet only works inside code that already has `byte[] candidate` and the necessary imports; the standalone runnable example is in section 5.

**`errors.isEmpty()`** means **the Class-File API verifier did not detect any errors in that check**, not "it has been proven that the entire application runs correctly." If there are multiple errors, the API returns a list of the errors found, rather than just returning a boolean.

### Does a `VerifyError` in the list mean the JVM just rejected the class?

Not necessarily. The type `java.lang.VerifyError` is also a subclass of `LinkageError`; the JVM can **throw** `VerifyError` when loading/linking an inconsistent class. However, `ClassFile.verify(...)` is designed to **return** error objects in `List<VerifyError>` when performing an active check. Do not confuse an element in the list with the JVM having attempted to define the class and thrown an error at runtime.

For example:

```text
ClassFile.verify(candidate) → [VerifyError, VerifyError]  (active check)
JVM define/load candidate  → may throw VerifyError        (runtime process)
```

These two paths have different contexts: the Class-File API verifier is inspecting your data; the JVM verifier operates during actual class definition/linking.

### `parse(...)` is not synonymous with `verify(...)` either

`ClassFile.parse(byte[])` reads the class structure into a `ClassModel`, and the Class-File API uses **lazy parsing**. Therefore, a file with a readable header can still contain corrupted parts that are only detected when deeply accessing a method, attribute, or instruction. The API may throw `IllegalArgumentException` when parsing or when accessing a malformed model.

`verify(...)` is a deeper consistency-checking step, but **you should not write code that only expects `List<VerifyError>`**: a severely malformed file, an unsupported version, or a resolver failure can cause the parse/verify operation to **throw an exception**, instead of returning a normal error list. When building tools, separate two states:

1. **Cannot be parsed**: exception during reading/parsing or resolver/build.
2. **Parsed but has verification errors**: `verify` returns a non-empty list.

Both must prevent the artifact from being released.

## 3. Different checking layers in a pipeline

| Layer | Primary question | Example errors | What does success guarantee? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **File reading/transport** | Does the file exist, are the bytes the exact version to check? | Incomplete read, wrong artifact | Only guarantees a set of bytes was obtained |
| **Parse/syntax** | Are the `.class` structure, constant pool, version, attributes readable? | Wrong magic, truncated data, bad index | Only guarantees the parsed parts have usable structure |
| **Build/transform** | Can the builder write the class file to bytes? | Unbound label, unexportable code configuration | Not enough to conclude the code is valid |
| **`ClassFile.verify`** | Does the bytecode/class file pass the API's checks? | Inconsistent type/stack/branch/frame | No errors found according to the verifier and context of that run |
| **JVM define/verify/link** | Does the actual JVM accept the class in this loader/module? | `VerifyError`, `ClassFormatError`, `UnsupportedClassVersionError`, `NoClassDefFoundError` | Not certain that every lazy reference or every code path has been exercised |
| **Execution/semantics** | Does the method perform the right business logic and observable constraints? | Wrong return value, lost exception, duplicate span | Only checks behavior that was executed in tests |

The layers above **complement one another** rather than replacing each other.

A method with valid bytecode that returns `0` when business logic requires returning `totalPrice` can still report **no errors** from `verify`. The verifier does not know domain rules, product API contracts, or trace/span expected counts.

## 4. Which exact bytes to check?

Suppose you have the following code:

```java
ClassFile cf = ClassFile.of();
ClassModel sourceModel = cf.parse(sourceBytes);
byte[] transformed = cf.transformClass(
        sourceModel, ClassTransform.ACCEPT_ALL);
```

`ClassTransform.ACCEPT_ALL` only passes elements through for the builder to reconstruct the file, with no logic modifying methods. Even so, it still produces **a new output byte array**; constant-pool entry ordering, certain attributes, or stack maps may change in representation.

To check the output:

```java
List<VerifyError> errors = cf.verify(transformed);
```

**Do not stop at**:

```java
// Insufficient: the source may be fine, but the transform below can introduce errors.
cf.verify(sourceBytes);
byte[] transformed = cf.transformClass(
        cf.parse(sourceBytes), myTransform);
// ... releasing transformed without verifying it.
```

If another transformer processes `transformed` afterward, the output of that second transformer must also be verified before release. With multiple agents, an individual transformer only controls the bytes **it returns**, and cannot guarantee that the final bytes after all JVM transformers are valid.

### Example when writing an artifact

```java
byte[] candidate = cf.transformClass(model, transform);
List<VerifyError> errors = cf.verify(candidate);

if (errors.isEmpty()) {
    Files.write(outputPath, candidate);
    // For build tools, you can verify(outputPath) and compare file hashes.
}
```

This snippet is a local example and requires declaring `cf`, `model`, `transform`, `outputPath`, and the appropriate imports. If the pipeline also includes packaging/shading/obfuscation steps, you must check **the artifact after the final step**, not only the bytes before packaging into a JAR.

## 5. Standalone experiment with JDK 24+: build → transform → verify → load

This experiment creates a new class using the Class-File API, transforms it via `ClassTransform.ACCEPT_ALL` to produce the release byte array, checks it as a model/byte array/path, saves it to disk, and uses a dedicated class loader to load the generated class. No libraries outside the JDK are used.

### 5.1. Requirements

- Use **JDK 24 or later** (`java` and `javac` from the same JDK or compatible version).
- `--enable-preview` is not needed when using the **official** Class-File API from JDK 24.
- `--add-modules` is not needed for `java.base`, because `java.lang.classfile` belongs to the `java.base` module.
- Run from a working directory with permission to create the `generated/` file/directory.

Check:

```bash
java -version
javac -version
```

The output depends on the installed JDK; you must see version **24 or newer**. With JDK 17, the program will not compile due to the missing `java.lang.classfile` package, not because of invalid Java syntax.

### 5.2. A complete single file: `VerifyGeneratedClass.java`

```java
import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile;
import java.lang.classfile.ClassModel;
import java.lang.classfile.ClassTransform;
import java.lang.constant.ClassDesc;
import java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs;
import java.lang.constant.MethodTypeDesc;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;

public final class VerifyGeneratedClass {

    // Define the new class directly from byte[] to test JVM runtime.
    private static final class IsolatedLoader extends ClassLoader {
        Class<?> define(byte[] bytes) {
            return defineClass(null, bytes, 0, bytes.length);
        }
    }

    private static void check(String stage, List<VerifyError> problems) {
        System.out.println(stage + "=" + problems.size());
        if (!problems.isEmpty()) {
            for (VerifyError problem : problems) {
                System.err.println(problem);
            }
            throw new IllegalStateException(
                    "Class verification failed at " + stage);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ClassFile cf = ClassFile.of();
        ClassDesc name = ClassDesc.of("demo.VerifiedGreeting");

        // Generate a public class with a constructor and a static message() method.
        byte[] built = cf.build(name, builder -> builder
                .withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_SUPER)
                .withMethodBody(
                        ConstantDescs.INIT_NAME,
                        ConstantDescs.MTD_void,
                        ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC,
                        code -> code.aload(0)
                                .invokespecial(
                                        ConstantDescs.CD_Object,
                                        ConstantDescs.INIT_NAME,
                                        ConstantDescs.MTD_void)
                                .return_())
                .withMethodBody(
                        "message",
                        MethodTypeDesc.of(ConstantDescs.CD_String),
                        ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC,
                        code -> code.ldc("HELLO").areturn()));

        // Parse the newly generated bytes back into a ClassModel.
        ClassModel model = cf.parse(built);
        check("model-errors", cf.verify(model));

        // Rebuild bytes via ClassTransform: this is the artifact to be released.
        byte[] candidate = cf.transformClass(
                model, ClassTransform.ACCEPT_ALL);
        check("candidate-errors", cf.verify(candidate));

        // Write and re-check the exact file just written.
        Path target = Path.of("generated", "demo", "VerifiedGreeting.class");
        Files.createDirectories(target.getParent());
        Files.write(target, candidate);
        check("disk-errors", cf.verify(target));

        // Final test step: JVM actually defines the class and invokes the public method.
        Class<?> loaded = new IsolatedLoader().define(candidate);
        Object answer = loaded.getMethod("message").invoke(null);
        System.out.println("runtime=" + answer);
    }
}
```

**Why is this program a good test?**

- `ClassFile.of().build(...)` actually **creates a new class file** from `ClassDesc`, `ClassBuilder`, and `CodeBuilder`; it does not merely read an existing file.
- The constructor calls `Object.<init>` properly; `message()` pushes a constant string onto the operand stack and uses `areturn`, matching the descriptor `()Ljava/lang/String;`.
- `ClassTransform.ACCEPT_ALL` demonstrates that checking **the final output** after a transform pass differs from only verifying the source model.
- It tests **all three overloads**: `verify(ClassModel)`, `verify(byte[])`, and `verify(Path)`.
- `IsolatedLoader` defines the exact `candidate` array, without accidentally picking up a class of the same name from the class path. `defineClass(null, ...)` reads the class name from the bytes.
- `loaded.getMethod("message").invoke(null)` uses reflection to invoke the public **static** method. It tests the JVM runtime level that standalone `verify` does not represent.
- It does not use `Class.forName("demo.VerifiedGreeting")` via the system class loader, so it does not collide with other build outputs or JARs.

### 5.3. Run commands

In the directory containing `VerifyGeneratedClass.java`:

```bash
javac -encoding UTF-8 VerifyGeneratedClass.java
java VerifyGeneratedClass
```

**Expected stdout on a normal JDK 24+:**

```text
model-errors=0
candidate-errors=0
disk-errors=0
runtime=HELLO
```

You can inspect the written artifact using the JDK tool:

```bash
javap -v generated/demo/VerifiedGreeting.class
```

`javap -v` shows the header, constant pool, methods, access flags, Code, and attributes of the class. It is a **structural/bytecode inspection tool for investigation**, and cannot replace the full combination of `ClassFile.verify(...)`, JVM load testing, and business-logic tests.

### 5.4. Why not compare `built` and `candidate` with `Arrays.equals`?

A transform that is an identity **semantically** is not required to preserve every single byte of the class file. The API may apply options for constant pool, stack maps, attribute processing, or data ordering. Two different byte arrays can still represent a class with the same behavior. Conversely, two identical byte arrays do not prove they are valid for the target runtime.

If you want byte-for-byte comparison to detect build regressions, use a hash on **the specific artifact** and clearly define reproducibility requirements. To verify structure, use `verify`; to verify semantics, use runtime tests.

## 6. A negative example: a parse error is not the same as an empty `verify` result

Suppose the `candidate` bytes have one byte modified in the magic number. A class file must start with `CAFEBABE` in the first four bytes. If you change the first byte to `0x00`, it is no longer a valid class file.

The following snippet illustrates how to investigate this, **and does not need to be added to the runnable program in section 5**:

```java
// Within a scope that already has byte[] candidate and ClassFile cf:
byte[] broken = candidate.clone();
broken[0] = 0;

try {
    ClassModel malformed = cf.parse(broken);
    // With a lazy parser, deep access may be required to detect certain errors.
    System.out.println(malformed.thisClass());
} catch (IllegalArgumentException malformedClass) {
    System.out.println("class file cannot be parsed");
}
```

The example does not print a fixed stdout for every malformed class file, because the point of error detection and the message depend on the corrupted data and when the parser accesses it. **Do not assume every format error becomes a `VerifyError` element in the list.** Some errors lack enough valid structure to run the verification pass to completion.

Similarly, a class file truncated in the middle of the constant pool, missing bytes of the `Code` attribute, or declaring a version beyond the runtime's capability can prevent `parse`/`verify` from completing normally. Catch the error, classify it, and do not release.

### Two states that must not be equated

```text
cf.verify(bytes).isEmpty() == true
    → Verification completed, no errors reported.

cf.parse(bytes) or cf.verify(bytes) throws an exception
    → Verification did NOT complete; you have no right to declare PASS.
```

Never write a `catch (Exception ignored) { return true; }` block to ignore failure cases. A build pipeline should *fail closed* if it cannot check the artifact.

## 7. What does `verify` actually check?

By design, `ClassFile.verify` aims to detect **class-file/bytecode verification** errors that can be analyzed from the class structure and hierarchy information of the referenced types. Typical areas of concern include:

- Are descriptors and bytecode structures valid for the method/class context?
- Are the operand stack and local variable type analysis results consistent across branches?
- Are instructions such as `ireturn`, `areturn`, `invokevirtual`, and `invokestatic` used compatibly with the expected type information?
- Do branch targets and exception handlers form valid control flow, consistent with verifiable stack-map frames?
- Are attributes and constant-pool references consistent enough to read/verify?

The list above describes **the kinds of invariants of a bytecode verifier**, not a guarantee that a given version of `ClassFile.verify` will diagnose **every corrupted variant**, across every custom class loader, every attribute extension, and every JVM vendor.

A method can pass type verification and still call the wrong helper, forget to record a span, return a business error, or leak information. Format validity is **different** from program correctness.

### Stack-map frames and control flow

For modern class files, `StackMapTable` helps the verifier check type states at required control-flow points. The Class-File API provides `ClassFile.StackMapsOption` and generation/reuse mechanisms. The relevant default is `STACK_MAPS_WHEN_REQUIRED`.

If a transformer adds `if` branches, `try/catch` blocks, or shifts code offsets, it can affect branch labels, exception handlers, and stack maps. Example configuration:

```java
ClassFile cf = ClassFile.of(
        ClassFile.StackMapsOption.GENERATE_STACK_MAPS);
```

This only requests stack-map generation in the output; it **does not automatically guarantee** that the body logic is correct, that every dependent class can be resolved, or that exception handling preserves its meaning. `StackMapsOption.DROP_STACK_MAPS` can cause the output to fail verification when a method has branches/handlers without supplying valid frames itself. Do not relax verification requirements to "hide" stack-map errors.

## 8. The biggest limit: the JVM also depends on runtime context

Imagine a class with an instruction calling:

```text
invokestatic com/example/Helper.sendEvent:()V
```

The instruction structure, descriptor, and operand stack themselves may be valid; yet at actual runtime, the class loader might **not find** `com.example.Helper`. In that case, using the class can cause `NoClassDefFoundError` or a related linkage error. `ClassFile.verify` is not a check that "every dependency on the execution path is present in production."

Other scenarios outside what an empty verify result can guarantee:

| Scenario | Why additional checks are needed |
| --- | --- |
| **Missing runtime class/helper** | The actual resolver or class loader does not see the class when linking or calling the method |
| **Wrong access/module graph** | `IllegalAccessError`, `InaccessibleObjectException`, or linkage errors can arise from permissions/named modules |
| **Wrong method descriptor in dependency** | `NoSuchMethodError`, `NoSuchFieldError`, `IncompatibleClassChangeError` can occur |
| **Dynamic bootstrap/linking** | `invokedynamic`, method handles, and bootstrap methods can fail at link time |
| **Business behavior** | The verifier does not know the right result for an order, transaction, or domain rule |
| **Concurrency** | Races, deadlocks, lost thread context, and double instrumentation are not detected by the verifier alone |
| **Performance** | A valid probe can still increase latency, allocation, or cause recursion/log floods |
| **Data security** | Valid bytecode can still read/write sensitive data in violation of policy |
| **JVM version compatibility** | The released file may use a major/minor version or features unsupported by the target runtime |
| **Redefine/retransform limits** | Class bytes valid for initial loading are not necessarily a valid replacement for an already loaded class |

Therefore, `ClassFile.verify(...)` should be **one step in a control chain**, not the entire production-readiness standard.

## 9. Custom class loaders and `ClassHierarchyResolver`

This is an important angle for Java agents.

To compute or verify the types of stack-map frames, the Class-File API may need to understand the superclass/interface relationships of types used in the bytecode. The Class-File API allows supplying **`ClassFile.ClassHierarchyResolverOption`**.

The default resolver may rely on **reflection and the system class loader** to look up hierarchies. In applications using custom class loaders, plugin loaders, servlet containers, framework module layers, or classes currently being transformed but not yet defined, the assumption that "every type is in the system loader" can be wrong. The resolver can also trigger class loading that the agent **does not want to trigger prematurely**.

This leads to three warnings:

1. **False tool failure**: failing to resolve a class in the application's loader even though the actual JVM can see the class at runtime.
2. **Wrong hierarchy**: resolving a class with the same name from a different loader, leading to misunderstood subtype relationships. In the JVM, class identity is based on name **and defining class loader**.
3. **Side effects**: using reflection to resolve types can cause classes to load while handling a class-load callback, increasing the risk of recursion/reentrancy or initialization errors.

When building an agent, you can configure:

```java
// Configuration illustration; the resolver must be implemented by the application.
ClassFile cf = ClassFile.of(
        ClassFile.ClassHierarchyResolverOption.of(resolver));
```

**`resolver` is not a built-in variable in the JDK**. This example shows where to plug in a `ClassHierarchyResolver` implementation that understands the target's class loaders/classpath/module layers. If reliable hierarchy data is unavailable, **do not blindly assume every type is `java.lang.Object`** just to force the verifier or stack-map generation to "PASS."

When reading logs, also record the loader, module, package, class version, resolver options, and which transformation chain ran. Differences between build and runtime environments can cause an artifact that verifies cleanly in CI to break on the server.

## 10. Attributes and options: verify does not guarantee all metadata remains intact

A class file contains many attributes besides Code, for example:

- `RuntimeVisibleAnnotations`, `RuntimeInvisibleAnnotations`, and parameter/type-use annotations.
- `Signature` (generic information), `MethodParameters`, `NestHost`/`NestMembers`.
- `Record`, `PermittedSubclasses`, `BootstrapMethods`.
- `LineNumberTable`, `LocalVariableTable`, `StackMapTable`.
- Custom attributes from frameworks/tools.

When transforming, some attributes have **data dependencies** on the constant pool, code offsets, labels, or other structures. If an agent modifies instructions and then copies attributes inappropriately, the result may no longer be correct. Options such as `AttributesProcessingOption`, `AttributeMapperOption`, `LineNumbersOption`, and `DebugElementsOption` affect how metadata is kept/dropped/recreated.

`ClassFile.verify(...)` is not a *semantic preservation* comparison between input and output: a transformer that accidentally strips important framework `RuntimeVisibleAnnotations` or debug line numbers can still produce a class that verifies. You must have **separate checks** to ensure required metadata is preserved.

Example post-check:

```text
Does the class still have the required name/superclass/interfaces?
Are core fields/methods/descriptors intact?
Are annotations needed by frameworks preserved?
Do debug attributes still meet diagnostic requirements?
Is the probe inserted in the right place without duplication?
Are the class's module/loader still appropriate?
```

Not every attribute must be kept (a transform may intentionally drop some), but whatever **was not meant to be altered** must be verified by its own rules.

## 11. Using `ClassFile.verify` in a Java agent

Inside the `ClassFileTransformer.transform(...)` callback, an agent can receive `classfileBuffer`, build a new `byte[]` with the Class-File API, and must decide **whether to return the bytes or skip**.

Recommended flow:

```text
transform(module, loader, name, classBeingRedefined, domain, original)
    ├─ Filter class: matching package/module/loader?
    ├─ Parse original with Class-File API
    ├─ Apply ClassTransform → candidate
    ├─ Verify candidate (with appropriate resolver)
    │      ├─ errors / exception → log diagnostics, do not emit candidate
    │      └─ no errors
    ├─ Check agent invariants (methods/metadata/probes)
    └─ return candidate
```

Illustrative **body snippet**, not a complete Java agent:

```java
// Inside transform(...) with className, classfileBuffer, myTransform
// and a suitably configured ClassFile cf.
if (!"com/example/Orders".equals(className)) {
    return null;
}

byte[] candidate = cf.transformClass(
        cf.parse(classfileBuffer),
        myTransform);

List<VerifyError> problems = cf.verify(candidate);
if (!problems.isEmpty()) {
    for (VerifyError problem : problems) {
        System.err.println(problem);
    }
    return null; // Discard changes from the current transformer.
}
return candidate;
```

`myTransform` is a `ClassTransform` that the agent **must provide itself**; the code above cannot run standalone and should not be copied verbatim into production. If parse/transform/verify throws an exception, the agent needs **a clear handling policy**: log the exact class + phase, emit diagnostic metrics, and decide whether to skip or fail according to system requirements. Do not swallow errors so operators are unaware that instrumentation was skipped.

In a Java `ClassFileTransformer`, returning `null` means **the current transformer provides no new class bytes**. It does not erase transformations returned by earlier transformers. If the agent requires a mandatory observability feature, silently returning `null` can leave the application running without a required signal; choosing fail-open or fail-closed must be based on operational specifications.

### Performance notes

The verifier performs analysis, so calling it on **every class** and in every class-load callback can consume CPU/memory. Practical guidance:

- Strictly filter classes before parsing/verifying, and avoid instrumenting the agent's own internal classes.
- Test transformed templates/classes separately in build/CI.
- For a live agent, measure real overhead; verify only outputs produced by the agent or choose sampling/appropriate policies when the risk is accepted.
- Do not dump entire class files or messages containing sensitive information into logs.
- Have a mechanism to disable/quarantine a transform that fails repeatedly instead of looping continuously.

**Correctness before optimization:** do not drop all verification just because a callback is slow; first define the scope and measure the actual cost.

## 12. `verify` does not replace `redefineClasses`/`retransformClasses` limits

For classes already in use by the JVM, Java instrumentation imposes additional constraints. A newly generated class file that **verifies successfully** may still **not be allowed** to replace an already loaded class via `Instrumentation.retransformClasses` or `redefineClasses`.

For example, adding new fields/methods or changing method signatures, modifiers, inheritance, or certain structural attributes may be **invalid for redefinition**, even when that class is completely valid to load from scratch. `ClassFile.verify` checks the validity of class-file bytes, not a tool for confirming all JVM **compatibility conditions with the prior definition**.

Therefore, two independent steps are required:

```text
candidate bytes
   ├─ ClassFile.verify(candidate) → class file / bytecode verification
   └─ redefine/retransform policy → compare old/new structure + JVM capabilities
                                    + current JVM restrictions
```

At runtime:

- `Instrumentation.isRetransformClassesSupported()` and the corresponding manifest capability must allow retransformation.
- `Instrumentation.isModifiableClass(clazz)` must hold for the specific class.
- The output after the entire transformer chain must be valid.
- A retransform/redefine request can fail due to `UnmodifiableClassException`, format errors, schema changes, or JVM-specific reasons.
- Active stack frames may continue executing the old method version; static fields are not automatically reset just because of retransformation.

If a transformer returns a candidate and the JVM refuses to install it, a "verify OK" log **is not confirmation that retransformation succeeded**.

## 13. Designing a multi-layered test suite for generated bytes

A workflow for a professional instrumentation library should separate the stages:

### Phase A — before generating bytecode

1. Confirm the **class-file version** to be emitted is compatible with the target JDK. An API running on a newer JDK can generate class files unreadable by an older runtime if you do not manage the version.
2. Ensure the target class information comes from the right class loader and module.
3. Clearly define the transform: what probe to add, in which method, and what data to preserve.
4. Choose an appropriate resolver/hierarchy to build stack maps.
5. Enforce limits on class size, method count, branch count, and callback processing time.

### Phase B — after generation

1. Keep the exact `byte[] candidate` after the transform.
2. Call `ClassFile.verify(candidate)` on **the exact output array**; distinguish list errors from parse/verify exceptions.
3. Check invariants: class name, method descriptors, annotations, generic signatures, `Nest`/`Record` metadata, helper references, and duplicate-probe guards.
4. If it is a build artifact, write `candidate` to the final file/JAR entry and verify **that exact file/entry**.
5. Log at least the class name, class-loader context, transform version, error count, and artifact hash; avoid emitting bytes that may contain sensitive data.

### Phase C — in the target JVM

1. Use the same JVM/JDK vendor, module graph, and class loaders as production.
2. Actually load/define the class; for agents, test a permitted load/retransform/redefine cycle.
3. Exercise all methods, success/error branches, and exception handling.
4. Verify before/after business logic, trace/span parents, metric cardinality, thread-local context, and overhead.
5. Use regression tests for agent combinations to detect transformation-chain conflicts.

### Phase D — after deployment

1. Alert when class instrumentation is skipped due to verification errors.
2. Distinguish JVM verify errors from bootstrap/link, class loader, access, or business-logic errors.
3. Have an appropriate rollback: for an agent modifying already-loaded classes, merely "removing the transformer" does not automatically remove installed probes.
4. Maintain documentation on verified class-file versions, options, and JDKs.

## 14. Error classification table when reading logs

| Symptom | Possible origin | Investigation direction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `IllegalArgumentException` on `parse` | Malformed bytes, unsupported version; lazy model hit a bad section | Check header, major/minor version, constant pool/attributes |
| `IllegalArgumentException` on `build/transform` | Unbound label, unexportable structure, or stack-map generation error | Check builder usage, branch labels, transform order |
| `verify(bytes)` returns non-empty list | Class file/bytecode failed the performed checks | Read each `VerifyError`, map to method/code, halt release |
| `verify(Path)` throws `IOException` | Unreadable file, wrong path, filesystem error | Check artifact path, permissions, file-writing pipeline |
| `VerifyError` at load time | JVM verifier rejected class definition | Compare actual bytes received by JVM, loader, flags, and `StackMapTable` |
| `ClassFormatError` | JVM does not recognize the class file as a valid structure | Check format/attributes/constant pool/version |
| `UnsupportedClassVersionError` | Runtime does not support the class-file version | Compare major version with the running JDK |
| `NoClassDefFoundError` | Class dependency missing or definition failed | Check class path/module path, defining loader, and cause |
| `NoSuchMethodError`/`IllegalAccessError` | Linkage to runtime API differs from assumptions | Check descriptor, access flags, module graph, and dependency version |
| `BootstrapMethodError` | Dynamic call site/constant linkage failed | Check bootstrap method, method handle, loader |
| `UnmodifiableClassException` on retransform | Class not modifiable or operation unsupported | Check JVM capabilities, `isModifiableClass`, redefine limits |
| Bytecode verifies OK but logic is wrong | Probe misplaced, return/throw altered, or helper has side effects | Run unit/integration tests and compare behavior with/without agent |

### A diagnostic rule worth remembering

**"JVM reports `VerifyError`" does not mean "`ClassFile.verify` had a bug during the CI check."** The two environments may use different class loaders/hierarchies, the final bytes may have been modified by another transform, or the tool may have verified bytes other than what the JVM actually received. Before fixing bytecode, **confirm the exact same artifact** and the same context.

## 15. Common misconceptions

1. **"`build(...)` didn't throw, so the class is valid."** False: the builder does not perform all consistency checks; you must verify the output.
2. **"`parse(...)` succeeded, meaning method bytecode is valid."** False: the parser is lazy, and verification is a separate step.
3. **"`verify` returns a boolean."** False: all three overloads return `List<VerifyError>`.
4. **"No `VerifyError` in the list proves the application runs correctly."** False: JVM loading/linking, business logic, and performance must be tested separately.
5. **"Only verifying input from `javac` is enough."** Insufficient: the bytecode **after transformation** is the output to be released.
6. **"After calling `verify(model)`, there's no need to check the generated bytes."** Insufficient: the model can differ from the final output and subsequent steps can still modify it.
7. **"ClassFile API has been available since Java 17."** False. The official standard API is from JDK 24; use JDK 24+.
8. **"Every error is always in the list."** False: parse, I/O, generation, or the resolver can throw an exception.
9. **"`StackMapTable` is always automatically right without hierarchy."** False: the resolver and actual loader context matter, especially in agents.
10. **"Verify OK means retransform can add fields."** False: redefinition limits are a separate condition.
11. **"The verifier checks whether framework annotations were lost."** It is not a semantic-preservation check; separate invariant checks are needed.
12. **"Removing the transformer reverts the class to the original."** False: bytes already defined by the JVM have their own lifecycle.
13. **"The default resolver always works with custom loaders."** False: the system loader may not see application classes.
14. **"A class file with changed bytes that still verifies is guaranteed equivalent to the source."** False: verification checks validity, not business intent.
15. **"Using `-noverify` to bypass errors is a fix."** False; disabling/bypassing verification does not solve transformation bugs and carries security and operational risks. Fix the bytecode instead.

## 16. Self-check exercises

**Q1.** Why must `ClassFile.verify(candidate)` be called after `transformClass(...)`?  
**A:** Because builders/transforms can produce inconsistent bytes; verifying the source before transformation does not check the final output.

**Q2.** What does `ClassFile.verify(byte[])` return when no errors are detected?  
**A:** An empty `List<VerifyError>`, not `true`.

**Q3.** Does a file with a wrong magic number necessarily produce a `VerifyError` in the list?  
**A:** No. The parser/verifier may throw an exception because the file can no longer be parsed.

**Q4.** Why does the example require JDK 24+ instead of using JDK 17?  
**A:** `java.lang.classfile` is a standard API starting in JDK 24; JDK 17 does not provide this package.

**Q5.** A helper class is missing at runtime, but the method bytecode has a valid stack. Does an empty `verify` result prove linking will succeed?  
**A:** No. You must test against the actual class loader/module graph and real dependency set.

**Q6.** With a custom class loader, why can the default class hierarchy resolver be dangerous?  
**A:** It may fail to see classes in the application's loader, misread type identity, or trigger unintended auxiliary class loading.

**Q7.** A class has a new method and verifies successfully. Can it be used to retransform an already loaded class?  
**A:** You cannot conclude that; retransformation has restrictions on schema changes.

**Q8.** How do `verify(ClassModel)` and `verify(Path)` differ?  
**A:** `Model` checks the in-memory model you hold; `Path` checks the actual file read from disk, which can catch errors in the file-writing step that differ from the model.

**Q9.** Why does the example still call `IsolatedLoader.define(...)` when all three verify calls return empty lists?  
**A:** To test the next layer: that the actual JVM can define and execute a method from the candidate bytes.

**Q10.** If agent C further transforms the bytes after agent B verifies, is B's verify result enough to guarantee the final bytes received by the JVM?  
**A:** No. B only checks the output at B's layer; the bytes after C need their own checking process or runtime verification.

## 17. References

- [JDK 25 — `ClassFile`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/classfile/ClassFile.html): `parse`, `build`, `transformClass`, `verify(byte[])`, `verify(ClassModel)`, `verify(Path)`.
- [JDK 25 — `java.lang.classfile` package](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/classfile/package-summary.html): lazy models, builders, verification, and the note on **no default consistency-checking** when building.
- [JDK 25 — `ClassTransform`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/classfile/ClassTransform.html): `ACCEPT_ALL` and how transformations are composed.
- [JDK 25 — `ClassFile.StackMapsOption`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/classfile/ClassFile.StackMapsOption.html): generating, keeping, dropping stack maps and verifier consequences.
- [JDK 25 — `ClassFile.ClassHierarchyResolverOption`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/classfile/ClassFile.ClassHierarchyResolverOption.html): resolver for stack map generation/verification, class loader issues.
- [OpenJDK — JEP 484](https://openjdk.org/jeps/484): Class-File API becomes an official API in JDK 24.
- [JVMS — The Class File Format](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se25/html/jvms-4.html) and [JVMS — Verification](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se25/html/jvms-4.html#jvms-4.10): foundations of class-file and bytecode verification.
- [JDK 25 — `Instrumentation`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.instrument/java/lang/instrument/Instrumentation.html): constraints of `redefineClasses` and `retransformClasses`.

**Takeaway:** `ClassFile.verify` is **a necessary active check for newly generated bytes**, not final proof that a class is compatible with every JVM, loader, and business requirement. Always verify **the final candidate**, properly classify parse/verify/build errors, preserve required metadata, test in a real JVM, and check additional instrumentation limits before deployment.
